chapters.title: A sugar's functional group helps classify it
chapters.formula: Glucose: aldohexose; fructose: ketohexose; both C6H12O6
chapters.script: Welcome to Biomolecules. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. Carbohydrates include sugars and their larger assemblies. Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed into simpler carbohydrate units. An aldose has an aldehyde group in its open-chain representation; a ketose has a ketone. Glucose is an aldohexose and fructose a ketohexose: both have six carbons, but their carbonyl positions differ. Many sugars spend most of their time in cyclic forms in solution, so an open-chain formula is a useful representation rather than the only structure present. Ring formation creates an anomeric centre. Do not identify a carbohydrate solely from the often-used simple carbon and water composition pattern; some compounds fit it without being carbohydrates and some carbohydrate derivatives do not fit it. For glucose and fructose, six carbon atoms and the same overall composition do not imply the same functional group position. Classification combines the carbon count with the open chain carbonyl type. Ring drawings add a further distinction between alpha and beta forms at an anomeric centre. A formula comparison should therefore be followed by a connectivity check before naming a sugar.
points: Glucose · Aldose · 6
Fructose · Ketose · 6
Same formula · Different connectivity · Check structure

board.heading: A sugar's functional group helps classify it

chapters.title: Hydrolysis tells us the units in a disaccharide
chapters.formula: C12H22O11 + H2O -> two C6H12O6 units for these disaccharides
chapters.script: Sucrose contains glucose and fructose units. Maltose contains two glucose units, while lactose contains galactose and glucose. Joining two monosaccharides with a glycosidic bond has the net composition change of losing one water molecule; hydrolysis adds water and separates the units. Structural bonding details distinguish the three despite related overall formulas. A reducing sugar can access a reactive carbonyl form under the relevant test conditions. Sucrose has both anomeric centres involved in its linkage and is nonreducing before hydrolysis. Maltose and lactose retain a suitable free anomeric centre and are reducing. Fructose can respond in alkaline reducing-sugar tests through rearrangement even though it is a ketose. For one mole of sucrose hydrolysed completely, one mole each of glucose and fructose appears. One mole of maltose gives two moles of glucose instead. The total monosaccharide amount doubles, while the carbon inventory is conserved. Water participates in hydrolysis, so adding the masses of the isolated sugar units need not equal the original dry disaccharide mass alone.
points: Sucrose · Glucose + fructose · Nonreducing
Maltose · Glucose + glucose · Reducing
Lactose · Galactose + glucose · Reducing

chapters.title: Large carbohydrate chains are not all interchangeable
chapters.formula: Same monomer does not imply the same linkage or polymer properties
chapters.script: Starch and glycogen store glucose units, whereas cellulose has a structural role. Different linkage arrangements change properties even when the repeating monosaccharide is glucose. This is an example of why a monomer name alone cannot specify the behaviour of a polymer. The official Chemistry unit emphasizes the named monosaccharides and the constituent units of sucrose, maltose and lactose. Use larger polysaccharides as supporting context rather than claiming every biological polymer detail is required. For a hydrolysis question, track the type and number of released units, not simply whether the original substance has a sweet taste. Amylose is largely unbranched, while amylopectin and glycogen have branching. Cellulose uses a different glucose linkage arrangement that gives extended structural chains. Humans do not digest cellulose with the same enzymes used for starch. These contrasts connect molecular bonding with macroscopic properties without changing the identity of the glucose building block. Linkage and branching must accompany the monomer name in a comparison.
points: Starch · Storage · Glucose linkages
Glycogen · Storage · More branched
Cellulose · Structural · Different linkage

chapters.title: Amino acids join through peptide bonds
chapters.formula: Simple linear n-residue peptide: n-1 peptide bonds
chapters.script: A typical alpha-amino acid has amino and carboxyl groups associated with the same alpha carbon. Its side chain distinguishes it from other amino acids. In suitable aqueous conditions, it can exist as a zwitterion carrying both positive and negative charges; the dominant ionic form depends on p H and the side chain. A peptide bond is the amide linkage with a carbonyl carbon bonded to nitrogen formed between amino-acid residues. The net assembly of a simple linear chain of n amino acids forms n minus one peptide links and releases n minus one waters in a condensation bookkeeping model. Living synthesis is more elaborate than directly mixing free amino acids. Hydrolysis breaks the links and adds water. For five amino acid residues in one noncyclic linear chain, four joins are needed. That gives four peptide bonds and four net water losses in the simple bookkeeping model. A cyclic peptide or several separate chains would require different counting. Glycine has two hydrogens at its alpha carbon, unlike a typical amino acid with four distinct attached groups, so do not automatically assign every amino acid a stereogenic alpha carbon.
points: 5 residues · 4 · 4
6 residues · 5 · 5
n residues · n − 1 · n − 1

board.heading: Amino acids join through peptide bonds

chapters.title: Protein structure has four different levels
chapters.formula: Denaturation is not the same process as peptide-bond hydrolysis
chapters.script: Protein structure is described at four different levels. Primary structure gives the amino acid sequence along a polypeptide chain. Secondary structure describes recurring local backbone arrangements, including alpha helices and beta sheets, with hydrogen bonds playing an important stabilizing role. Tertiary structure is the complete three dimensional folding of one chain. Quaternary structure describes how several polypeptide subunits are arranged together. A single chain protein can have the first three levels without having quaternary structure. Keep the sequence separate from the way that sequence folds. Denaturation changes the folded organization and can reduce biological activity. It does not necessarily break peptide bonds or turn the whole protein into free amino acids. Heat and changes in chemical environment can disturb stabilizing interactions, but different proteins respond differently. Refolding is not guaranteed simply by restoring the original temperature. In a comparison question, identify whether the evidence concerns sequence, local backbone folding, the shape of one complete chain or the association of several chains. Loss of activity with an intact peptide backbone supports a folding change rather than complete hydrolysis.
points: Primary · Sequence · Backbone order
Secondary / tertiary · Local / whole-chain fold · Folding levels
Quaternary · Multiple subunits · More than one chain

board.heading: Protein structure has four different levels

chapters.title: Enzymes speed reactions without changing equilibrium
chapters.formula: Catalysis changes the pathway and rate, not K at fixed conditions
chapters.script: Enzymes are biological catalysts; most are proteins, though some catalytic RNA molecules also exist. A suitable active site helps bind substrates and provide a lower-barrier pathway. Specificity reflects structure and interactions, not an absolute promise that one enzyme acts on only one possible molecule. Like other catalysts, enzymes do not change the equilibrium constant for a reaction at the same conditions. Activity depends on factors such as temperature and p H, and extreme conditions can damage structure. More heat does not mean unlimited acceleration because the catalyst can lose its working form. An enzyme changes the barrier along a reaction pathway and can accelerate both directions toward equilibrium. It does not force a different final equilibrium composition merely by being a catalyst. Changing acidity or temperature can change both the chemical environment and the enzyme structure. Compare activity measurements only when the substrate amount, conditions and measured interval are appropriately controlled.
points: Alternative pathway · Barrier and rate · Equilibrium K
Working structure · Depends on conditions · No unlimited heating
Activity comparison · Control environment · Not just enzyme name

chapters.title: Vitamins and hormones play different roles
chapters.formula: Fat-soluble vitamin group: A, D, E, K; water-soluble: B group and C
chapters.script: Vitamins are needed in small amounts for normal biochemical functions. The usual classification places A, D, E and K among fat-soluble vitamins and the B group and C among water-soluble vitamins. These are families with distinct roles, not one interchangeable chemical. Hormones are chemical signals acting through suitable biological targets; some are peptides, some steroids and others have different structures. Insulin is a peptide-hormone example, whereas many steroid hormones derive from a different molecular framework. Vitamin classification and hormone classification answer different questions. Solubility places vitamins into broad groups; it does not state a universal molecular structure or biochemical role. A peptide hormone has amino acid residues joined in a chain, while a steroid hormone has a different carbon framework. Recognize insulin as a peptide example and keep the two classification systems separate during revision. Recognizing a family name does not uniquely determine every reaction or functional group. Compare the actual molecular framework when a structure is supplied rather than treating all biological signalling compounds as the same class.
points: Fat-soluble vitamins · A, D, E, K · Solubility group
Water-soluble vitamins · B group, C · Different families
Hormones · Insulin; steroids · Different frameworks

chapters.title: DNA and RNA are chains of nucleotides
chapters.formula: Nucleoside = base + sugar; nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate component
chapters.script: A nucleoside combines a nitrogenous base and a sugar. Adding a phosphate component gives a nucleotide, the building block of nucleic acids. DNA uses deoxyribose and typically the bases A, G, C and T; RNA uses ribose and usually A, G, C and U. The sugar-phosphate backbone joins units through phosphodiester links. In the elementary double-stranded DNA model, A pairs with T and G with C, with complementary antiparallel strands. DNA stores hereditary information, while RNA has roles in expressing and processing it. Complementary DNA base-count rules apply to a whole double-stranded sample; do not impose equal A and T on an arbitrary single RNA strand. If adenine accounts for thirty percent of a whole complementary double stranded DNA sample, thymine is also thirty percent. Forty percent remains for guanine plus cytosine, giving twenty percent each. This calculation uses complementarity over both strands. A single isolated strand can have unequal adenine and thymine counts, and RNA substitutes uracil for thymine in the usual elementary comparison.
points: Adenine · Given · 30%
Thymine · Matches A · 30%
Guanine / cytosine · Equal shares of rest · 20% each

chapters.title: Read the Fischer pattern of D-glucose
chapters.formula: Open chain: OH positions C2–C5 = right, left, right, right
chapters.script: A Fischer projection encodes stereochemistry and is not simply a vertical decorative formula. For open chain D glucose, place the aldehyde group at the top and the terminal hydroxymethyl group at the bottom. The hydroxyl positions from carbon two through carbon five are right, left, right and right. Horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds point away in this projection convention. Carbon one belongs to the aldehyde; carbon six belongs to the terminal hydroxymethyl group. The D label is assigned by the configuration at the highest numbered stereogenic centre in this standard comparison, which is carbon five here. It does not mean every hydroxyl lies on the right. Nor does D automatically predict positive optical rotation. Changing one stereogenic centre can give a different sugar; merely rotating a whole spatial molecule does not. The projection is a useful open chain representation even though aqueous glucose is mainly cyclic. Keep carbon numbering visible when connecting the chain to a ring so that the anomeric carbon can be identified correctly.
points: Carbon numbering · CHO at C1; CH₂OH at C6 · Six carbons
OH at C2, C3, C4, C5 · Right, left, right, right · D-glucose pattern
D label · Configuration at C5 here · Not optical-rotation sign

chapters.title: Distinguish alpha and beta glucose
chapters.formula: For D-glucopyranose: anomeric OH trans / cis to CH₂OH gives α / β
chapters.script: When glucose forms a six membered pyranose ring, the carbon five hydroxyl oxygen connects with the carbon one aldehyde carbon to make a cyclic hemiacetal. Carbon one becomes the anomeric centre. Two configurations are possible there while the other stereogenic centres retain their relationships. In the standard Haworth representation of D glucopyranose with the hydroxymethyl group drawn up, an anomeric hydroxyl drawn down is alpha and one drawn up is beta. More generally, compare the anomeric hydroxyl with the reference hydroxymethyl group: trans gives alpha and cis gives beta for this representation. The schematic highlights those groups and does not show every hydroxyl. The two anomers can interconvert through ring opening and closure in solution, producing mutarotation. They are not different molecular formulas and they are not simply two conformations of one unchanged anomeric configuration. Alpha and beta labels also do not mean the signs of optical rotation. A chair conformation supplies further three dimensional information beyond this simplified ring projection, which should not be treated as an exact planar molecular shape.
points: Ring formation · C5 oxygen joins C1 · C1 is anomeric
α-D-glucopyranose · OH down; CH₂OH up · Opposite sides
β-D-glucopyranose · OH up; CH₂OH up · Same side

chapters.title: Reducing ends and sugar hydrolysis
chapters.formula: Sucrose + H₂O → glucose + fructose; 342 + 18 = 180 + 180
chapters.script: A free anomeric hemiacetal can open to a carbonyl form and provides a useful way to identify a reducing end. Maltose and lactose retain a free anomeric centre and are reducing disaccharides in the usual comparison. Sucrose links the anomeric centres of its glucose and fructose units, so it lacks that free reducing end before hydrolysis. Its hydrolysis gives one mole of glucose and one mole of fructose per mole of sucrose. With rounded molar masses, three hundred forty two grams of sucrose reacts with eighteen grams of water to give one hundred eighty grams of each monosaccharide. The total product mass is three hundred sixty grams; water has become part of the products rather than mass appearing from nowhere. Fructose can give reducing test behaviour under suitable alkaline conditions despite its open chain ketone classification, so aldehyde naming alone is not the complete criterion. Distinguish a sugar before hydrolysis from the mixture produced afterward. A change in a test result can reveal a changed linkage or newly accessible reducing end.
points: Maltose / lactose · Free anomeric centre · Reducing
Sucrose before hydrolysis · Both anomeric centres linked · Nonreducing

chapters.title: Amino acids change charge with pH
chapters.formula: Glycine: +1 in acid; net 0 zwitterion; −1 in base
chapters.script: An amino acid contains groups that can gain or lose protons, so its predominant charge depends on p H. Glycine provides a simple example without an ionizable side chain. In sufficiently acidic solution, its amino group is protonated and its carboxyl group is mostly neutral, giving net charge plus one. In the intermediate zwitterionic form, the amino group remains positive while the carboxylate is negative, giving net charge zero. In sufficiently basic solution, the carboxylate remains negative and the amino group is neutral, giving net charge minus one. A zwitterion is therefore not a structure with no formal charges; it has opposite charges in the same molecule. At the isoelectric point, the average net charge is zero under the stated conditions. This does not mean every molecule has permanently lost both acid base functions. Amino acids with ionizable side chains need additional protonation states and cannot be analysed by copying glycine's pattern alone. Identify all ionizable groups, compare the p H with the relevant dissociation constants, and then add their charges.
points: Acidic glycine · NH₃⁺ and COOH · Net +1
Zwitterionic glycine · NH₃⁺ and COO⁻ · Net 0; internal charges
Basic glycine · NH₂ and COO⁻ · Net −1

chapters.title: Peptide direction and condensation mass
chapters.formula: Linear n-residue chain: n − 1 peptide links and n − 1 waters lost
chapters.script: A peptide bond joins a carboxyl carbon of one amino acid to the nitrogen of another, with loss of water in the simplified condensation account. A linear chain with five residues has four peptide links and loses four water molecules when assembled from those free amino acids. A cyclic chain has different end group bookkeeping, so the linear rule must be stated. Sequence is directional: glycine followed by alanine is not the same connectivity as alanine followed by glycine, although the two dipeptides have the same total composition. Write from the amino terminus to the carboxyl terminus in the usual sequence convention. Using illustrative rounded molar masses of seventy five for glycine and eighty nine for alanine, forming one dipeptide gives seventy five plus eighty nine minus eighteen, or one hundred forty six grams per mole. Hydrolysis reverses the water balance. This calculation concerns one condensation link, not the loss of an entire hydroxyl or amino group from the residue count. Distinguish sequence, number of residues, number of links and mass balance before comparing peptide formulas.
points: Five-residue linear chain · n − 1 links · 4 peptide links

chapters.title: DNA base percentages require a defined strand set
chapters.formula: Canonical paired double-stranded DNA: A = T and G = C overall
chapters.script: A DNA base percentage problem must say whether its data describe one strand or the complete paired molecule. For ordinary double stranded DNA with canonical complementary pairing, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine with cytosine. Across the complete two strand molecule, adenine and thymine counts are equal, and guanine and cytosine counts are equal. If adenine is thirty percent of all bases, thymine is also thirty percent, leaving forty percent shared equally between guanine and cytosine. Each of those is twenty percent. Take a molecule containing one thousand base pairs, hence two thousand individual bases. The counts are six hundred adenines, six hundred thymines, four hundred guanines and four hundred cytosines. There are six hundred A T pairs and four hundred G C pairs. Counting two hydrogen bonds per A T pair and three per G C pair gives two thousand four hundred in the standard pairing model. One isolated strand need not have equal adenine and thymine percentages. Mismatches, single stranded material or noncanonical chemistry require the stated model to be reconsidered. Hydrogen bond counts alone also do not determine a DNA melting temperature, which depends on more structural and solution factors.
points: A = 30% of all bases · T=30%; G=C=20% · Both strands counted together
1000 base pairs · 600 AT + 400 GC pairs · 2000 individual bases
Canonical H-bond count · 2×600 + 3×400 · 2400 hydrogen bonds

chapters.title: A nucleotide is not just a base or a nucleoside
chapters.formula: Base + sugar = nucleoside; addition of phosphate gives a nucleotide
chapters.script: The terms base, nucleoside and nucleotide identify different amounts of molecular structure. A nitrogenous base attached to a pentose sugar is a nucleoside. Including phosphate gives a nucleotide. In the familiar nucleic acid backbone, phosphodiester links connect the three prime position of one sugar with the five prime position associated with the next nucleotide. The primes distinguish sugar carbon numbering from the base numbering. DNA normally contains deoxyribose, whereas RNA contains ribose with a hydroxyl at the two prime position. That sugar difference is separate from the usual thymine versus uracil base comparison. For an unbranched linear strand containing ten nucleotide residues, there are nine internucleotide phosphodiester links. This does not mean there are always exactly nine phosphate groups: a terminal phosphate may add another, depending on how the ends are specified. A circular unbranched strand has a different link count because its ends join. Likewise, a double stranded DNA fragment consists of two covalently separate backbones connected through base pairing, not one continuous strand crossing between the bases. Count residues, links and terminal groups as distinct quantities before inferring composition.
points: Base + pentose · No phosphate required · Nucleoside
Nucleoside + phosphate · Sugar numbering uses primes · Nucleotide
10-residue linear strand · n − 1 internucleotide links · 9 links; ends specified separately

board.heading: A nucleotide is not just a base or a nucleoside

chapters.title: Protein denaturation and peptide hydrolysis are different
chapters.formula: Ordinary denaturation changes folding without normally cleaving the peptide backbone
chapters.script: Protein structure can change without cutting its amino acid sequence into separate molecules. Ordinary denaturation disrupts the interactions that maintain a native fold, so secondary, tertiary or quaternary organization and biological activity can be altered. The peptide backbone is not normally hydrolyzed merely by calling a process denaturation. Hydrolysis instead cleaves peptide bonds with chemical consumption of water and creates additional chain ends. For one ideal linear pentapeptide with no crosslinks, there are four peptide bonds. Complete hydrolysis consumes four water molecules per peptide molecule and gives five amino acid molecules. Breaking only one internal peptide bond gives two shorter peptide fragments, not five free amino acids. Disulfide bridges are another covalent connection: changing their oxidation state is distinct from cleaving an amide bond in the main chain. Real unfolding can be accompanied by aggregation, side reactions or loss of disulfide structure under particular treatments, so reversibility is not guaranteed. The useful distinction is which bonds and interactions are specified to change. Do not infer complete amino acid release or a new primary sequence solely from loss of native shape or enzyme activity.
points: Native fold disrupted · Peptide sequence usually retained · Denaturation ≠ full hydrolysis
Linear pentapeptide · 5 residues − 1 · 4 peptide bonds
Complete hydrolysis · Consume 4 H₂O per molecule · 5 free amino acid molecules

chapters.title: Estimate anomer fractions from supplied rotation data
chapters.formula: Rotationmix = fα rotationα + (1−fα) rotationβ
chapters.script: Mutarotation describes a change in optical rotation as an interconverting sugar mixture approaches its equilibrium composition. For a numerical glucose example, suppose the supplied specific rotations are plus one hundred twelve for the alpha form, plus eighteen point seven for the beta form, and plus fifty two point seven for the equilibrium mixture, all at matching measurement conditions. Use an explicit two form model that neglects minor open chain and other ring forms. Let the alpha fraction be f. The weighted rotation is one hundred twelve times f plus eighteen point seven times one minus f. Solving gives f equal to thirty four divided by ninety three point three, approximately zero point three six four. The beta fraction is therefore about zero point six three six. Both pure forms are dextrorotatory in this example, so the equilibrium is not a racemate with zero rotation. Alpha and beta describe the anomeric relationship, while D describes configuration relative to a reference structure; these labels do not by themselves state the sign of optical rotation for every sugar. The estimate uses the supplied rotations and additive mixture model, rather than claiming that every glucose solution at every temperature has exactly these fractions.
points: Given α +112; β +18.7 · Mixture +52.7 · Same measurement conditions
Two-form approximation · fβ = 1 − fα · β ≈ 63.6%; not a racemate

chapters.title: Fat-soluble vitamins have distinct functions
chapters.formula: A: vision; D: mineral balance; E: antioxidant; K: clotting-protein activation
chapters.script: Remembering that vitamins A D E and K are fat soluble is only the first classification step. Their physiological roles are distinct. Vitamin A contributes to the visual system, including the light sensitive retinal pigment system, and deficiency can cause night blindness. Vitamin D supports calcium and phosphate handling and normal bone mineralization; deficiency in children can cause rickets. Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant that helps protect cell membranes against oxidative damage. Vitamin K supports the activation of proteins involved in blood clotting, rather than serving as the physical material from which a clot is built. These are useful textbook associations, not a claim that every symptom identifies one vitamin or that each vitamin has only one function. None should be treated as a carbohydrate fuel simply because vitamins support normal metabolism. Solubility class also does not make the four molecules chemically identical or interchangeable. In a matching question, first read whether the prompt asks about solubility, a physiological role or a familiar deficiency association. Keeping those categories separate prevents a correct class label from becoming an incorrect functional answer.
points: A: visual system · D: calcium / phosphate handling · Night blindness / childhood rickets
E: antioxidant action · Helps protect cell membranes · Distinct from a fuel function
K: clotting-related proteins · Supports protein activation · A, D, E, K are fat soluble

chapters.title: Water-soluble vitamins and the storage exception
chapters.formula: B₁: cofactor metabolism; B₁₂: blood / nerves; C: collagen synthesis
chapters.script: Water soluble vitamins include the B group and vitamin C, but this category contains many different molecular functions. Thiamine, vitamin B one, contributes through its active cofactor form to important metabolic reactions, including carbohydrate metabolism. Beriberi is a familiar deficiency association. Vitamin B twelve supports normal red blood cell formation, DNA synthesis and nervous system function. Although it is water soluble, substantial body stores, especially in the liver, can last for years. Therefore the statement that every water soluble vitamin is immediately lost without storage is false. Vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid, is required for normal collagen synthesis; severe deficiency causes scurvy. Collagen is a structural protein, while vitamin C supports the biochemical processes needed to make it properly. The vitamin does not become a peptide residue merely because it helps protein formation. These examples are educational function and deficiency links, not diagnostic rules for an individual. In exam matching, use the named vitamin and the particular role together instead of treating every B vitamin as a substitute for every other one.

B₁₂: water soluble · Blood, DNA and nerve function · Liver stores can last years

chapters.title: Reading the D-fructose Fischer projection
chapters.formula: Open chain: C2=O; OH at C3 left, C4 right, C5 right
chapters.script: Compare the open chain Fischer projections of glucose and fructose without confusing carbonyl position with configuration. D fructose has six carbons, with terminal hydroxymethyl groups at carbon one and carbon six. Its carbonyl is a ketone at carbon two. In the standard projection with carbon one at the top, the hydroxyl groups at carbons three, four and five lie left, right and right, respectively. These three carbons are stereogenic in the open chain structure, whereas the carbonyl carbon is not a tetrahedral stereocentre. For the fixed unbranched two ketohexose connectivity, three independent stereocentres allow eight configurations. D fructose is one of them. The right hand hydroxyl at the highest numbered stereocentre, carbon five, provides the D reference here; D does not by itself predict the sign of optical rotation. Fischer horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds away. In solution, fructose also forms cyclic structures, where the former carbonyl carbon two becomes the anomeric centre. This open chain drawing is therefore a configuration reference, not a claim that every dissolved molecule remains in that form.

chapters.title: DNA reverse complement requires strand direction
chapters.formula: 5′-AGTC-3′ pairs with 3′-TCAG-5′; reverse complement is 5′-GACT-3′
chapters.script: A DNA complement question is incomplete until the strand directions are specified. Take the sequence adenine guanine thymine cytosine written from five prime to three prime. Directly beneath it, base pairing gives thymine cytosine adenine guanine, but that aligned complementary strand runs from three prime to five prime. If the answer must also be written from five prime to three prime, reverse the order of that complementary sequence. The answer is guanine adenine cytosine thymine. Merely replacing each letter without reversing gives an aligned complement in the opposite direction, not the requested five prime sequence. The short double stranded segment contains four base pairs and eight nucleotides in total. Two pairs are adenine thymine and two are guanine cytosine, giving ten interbase hydrogen bonds in the standard counting model. Each linear four nucleotide strand has three internucleotide phosphodiester connections, so the two backbones contain six such connections. That link count does not specify the exact number of terminal phosphate groups, because the end chemistry has not been given. Sequence direction, base pairing and backbone counting answer different parts of the same structural problem.

chapters.title: Glucose oxidation probes which terminal groups change
chapters.formula: Bromine-water model: gluconic acid; stronger nitric-acid model: glucaric / saccharic acid
chapters.script: Different reactions of glucose provide different structural evidence. In the familiar mild bromine water oxidation model, the accessible aldehyde end becomes a carboxyl group, giving the six carbon monocarboxylic product gluconic acid. In the stronger nitric acid oxidation comparison, both the aldehyde end and the terminal primary alcohol are oxidized, giving a six carbon dicarboxylic product called glucaric or saccharic acid. No carbon has been added in either change. Hydroxylamine reaction provides separate carbonyl evidence through oxime formation; it does not establish that every molecule remains in the open chain form in water. Acetylation to a pentaacetate supports the presence of five hydroxyl groups in glucose, while the cyclic equilibrium explains why a single static open chain drawing is incomplete. These observations answer different questions and should be combined rather than treated as interchangeable test names. For the supplied oxidation maps, first label carbon one and carbon six, then identify which end changes oxidation level. Product identity depends on the stated oxidant and conditions; a carboxylic acid name alone does not specify whether one or both terminal groups were oxidized.
points: Mild Br₂-water oxidation · C1 aldehyde → carboxyl · Gluconic acid; one COOH
Stronger nitric-acid comparison · C1 and terminal C6 oxidized · Glucaric / saccharic; two COOH

chapters.title: Epimers differ at one specified stereocentre
chapters.formula: D-Glucose / D-mannose: C2 epimers; D-glucose / D-galactose: C4 epimers
chapters.script: A pair of epimers differs in configuration at one stereogenic centre while retaining the same connectivity and the other configurations. Compare the open chain Fischer projections of three D aldohexoses. From carbon two through carbon five, glucose has hydroxyl positions right, left, right, right. Mannose has left, left, right, right, differing only at carbon two. Galactose has right, left, left, right, differing from glucose only at carbon four. Thus glucose and mannose are carbon two epimers, while glucose and galactose are carbon four epimers. Mannose and galactose differ at two centres, so they are diastereomers but not epimers of one another. All three remain D sugars because the highest numbered stereogenic centre has the same relative configuration. D does not mean positive optical rotation: configuration and the measured sign of rotation are separate descriptors. Anomers are the special cyclic comparison at the newly created anomeric centre, not a synonym for changing any Fischer position. Always identify the carbon number and projection convention before calling two sugar drawings an epimeric pair.

chapters.title: Disulfide cross-links are not peptide bonds
chapters.formula: 2 cysteine –SH → one –S–S– cross-link; no new peptide linkage
chapters.script: A protein can contain covalent links of different chemical types. A peptide linkage joins a carbonyl carbon to nitrogen along a polypeptide backbone. A disulfide instead joins sulfur atoms from two cysteine side chains after oxidation of their thiol groups. In formal atom bookkeeping, two thiols become one sulfur sulfur bond with loss of two hydrogen equivalents; this is not the condensation water loss used to count peptide assembly. Consider two separate linear tripeptide chains, each with one cysteine residue. Each chain has two peptide bonds, giving four in total. Joining the cysteine side chains with one interchain disulfide adds one cross link while leaving the peptide bond count at four. The connected structure still has two polypeptide backbones, not one newly lengthened six residue peptide backbone. Reducing that disulfide can separate the chains without hydrolysing their peptide bonds. Conversely, cutting a peptide bond is a backbone change and cannot be described solely as reducing sulfur. Distinguish side chain connectivity, chain count and backbone sequence before inferring which chemical treatment changed a protein sample.
points: Two linear tripeptide chains · 2 peptide bonds per chain · 4 peptide bonds total
One cysteine –SH per chain · Oxidation joins sulfur atoms · One interchain S–S cross-link
After disulfide formation · Backbone sequences unchanged · Still four peptide bonds

chapters.title: DNA backbone links and base-pair hydrogen bonds count differently
chapters.formula: Two intact linear N-nucleotide strands: 2(N−1) internal phosphodiester linkages
chapters.script: DNA contains both covalent backbone links and noncovalent interactions between complementary bases. Count them separately. Consider an intact linear double stranded fragment with ten base pairs, six adenine thymine pairs and four guanine cytosine pairs. There are twenty nucleotides, ten in each strand. Within each linear strand, ten nucleotide units are joined by nine internal phosphodiester bridges, giving eighteen internucleotide linkages in both backbones. A terminal phosphate does not create an extra bridge to a missing nucleotide. Using the standard paired base model, the six adenine thymine pairs contribute twelve hydrogen bonds and the four guanine cytosine pairs contribute twelve more, twenty four total. These hydrogen bonds are not the covalent links that hold each individual strand together. Count one internucleotide phosphodiester linkage per joining phosphate bridge, rather than confusing that bridge with each individual phosphorus oxygen ester bond. Circular closure, nicks or unpaired bases would change the assumptions. Strand separation can disrupt base pairing without requiring hydrolysis of all eighteen backbone linkages. Always state linearity, strand length and pairing before applying a counting shortcut.
points: 10 paired positions · 10 nucleotides per strand · 20 nucleotides total
Two intact linear backbones · 2 × (10−1) · 18 phosphodiester linkages

chapters.title: Glucose pentaacetate distinguishes free carbonyl evidence from a protected ring
chapters.formula: Glucose forms an oxime; glucose pentaacetate does not in the usual textbook comparison; five acetylated OH groups do not imply a free CHO group
chapters.script: Structural evidence must identify which form of a sugar is actually being tested. Unmodified glucose can react with hydroxylamine to give an oxime through its accessible carbonyl chemistry, even though cyclic hemiacetal forms predominate in water. Acetylation gives glucose pentaacetate, supporting the presence of five hydroxyl groups available for that transformation. In the usual textbook comparison, glucose pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine to give the analogous oxime. The protected cyclic structure lacks the freely available aldehyde behaviour assumed by a permanent open chain drawing. Acetylating the anomeric hydroxyl prevents the ordinary hemiacetal ring opening equilibrium without first changing the protected groups. This does not mean that glucose never has an open chain form, or that every acetate group is a new aldehyde. The two observations ask different questions: how many hydroxyl groups can be acetylated, and whether the tested derivative has an accessible carbonyl under the specified conditions. Hydrolysis or deprotection can change that answer, so the derivative and reaction conditions must remain explicit. Combine these observations with the other glucose evidence rather than treating one negative test as a complete structure proof.

chapters.title: Partial peptide fragments can distinguish identical total compositions
chapters.formula: Two Ala + one Gly: AAG, AGA, GAA; observed contiguous AG and GA fragments select AGA in the stated model
chapters.script: Complete hydrolysis can reveal peptide composition without fixing the order of residues. Suppose a supplied linear tripeptide contains two alanine residues and one glycine residue, with no modified residues or cyclization. Write sequences from amino terminus to carboxyl terminus and abbreviate alanine A and glycine G. The distinct composition compatible sequences are A A G, A G A and G A A; exchanging the two identical alanines does not make a fourth sequence. Now suppose controlled partial hydrolysis identifies both A G and G A as contiguous dipeptide fragments from the same pure tripeptide, with no rearrangement or transpeptidation in the stated evidence model. Only A G A contains both directed adjacent pairs. A A G contains A A and A G, while G A A contains G A and A A. All three candidates have two peptide bonds and the same mass computed from two free alanines plus one glycine minus two waters. Sequence evidence therefore adds information that mass and total amino acid counts cannot supply. Real sequence determination needs appropriate controls and fragment identification; this small overlap puzzle is a supporting inference exercise rather than a universal sequencing method.

chapters.title: Supporting pI calculation uses the two steps surrounding net zero charge
chapters.script: An ionizable side chain changes which dissociation steps surround an amino acid's net neutral form. Use a supporting dominant state calculation with supplied stepwise p K a values, rather than averaging every number automatically. For an aspartic acid model, the values are two point one, three point nine and nine point eight. Increasing p H removes protons through net charge states plus one, zero, minus one and minus two. The neutral state lies between the first two steps, so its approximate isoelectric point is their average, three point zero. For a lysine model with values two point two, nine point zero and ten point five, the successive net charges are plus two, plus one, zero and minus one. Here the neutral state lies between the last two steps, giving approximate isoelectric point nine point seven five. These are supplied illustrative constants and the usual adjacent state approximation, not universal values for every solvent and temperature. At the isoelectric point the average net charge is zero; charged groups within individual zwitterions still exist. Identify every ionizable group and the charge ladder before selecting the two constants.

chapters.title: Supporting RNA cleavage depends on the nearby two-prime hydroxyl
chapters.formula: RNA 2′-O⁻ attacks adjacent phosphate → 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate + downstream 5′-OH; DNA lacks the same 2′-OH pathway
chapters.script: The sugar difference between R N A and D N A affects backbone chemistry as well as molecular naming. In a supporting alkaline cleavage model, the two prime hydroxyl of an R N A ribose can lose a proton and provide a nearby oxygen nucleophile. That oxygen attacks the phosphorus of the adjacent three prime phosphate linkage within the same chain. The downstream phosphorus oxygen five prime connection breaks, leaving a two prime three prime cyclic phosphate on one fragment and a five prime hydroxyl on the other after proton transfer. The initial cleavage is an intramolecular transesterification; later opening of the cyclic phosphate can give additional hydrolysis products. This is different from merely separating complementary bases or denaturing a duplex. A D N A sugar has hydrogen rather than hydroxyl at two prime, so it cannot use this same neighbouring hydroxyl attack pathway. That distinction does not mean D N A is indestructible or that every R N A linkage cleaves at an identical rate. Sequence, conformation and conditions matter. For one specified internal cleavage in a linear chain, the number of covalently connected backbone pieces increases from one to two without creating or deleting nucleotide residues.
